content: The document provides detailed guidance on the regulations for the transport of infectious substances, applicable from January 1, 2019, as published by the World Health Organization (WHO). It outlines the terms under which the material can be copied, redistributed, or adapted for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. The WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, a disclaimer must be included, stating that the translation was not created by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The document emphasizes the importance of compliance with international regulations to ensure the safe transport of infectious substances. It highlights the role of biological agents in detecting and preventing outbreaks of emerging and highly infectious diseases, as well as reducing risks to international health security. Facilities handling biological agents are responsible for identifying, safely storing, and controlling these agents in adequately equipped facilities according to best practices. During the transport of materials containing biological agents, there is a risk of exposure to people and the environment. To mitigate this risk, international groups have developed recommendations and regulations for the packaging, marking, labeling, and documentation of infectious substances. One of the most widely referenced sets of recommendations is the UN Model Regulations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods, which provides a minimum set of provisions for the safe transport of dangerous goods, including infectious substances. These regulations are continuously reviewed and updated to reflect technical progress, new materials, and emerging safety requirements. The UN Model Regulations serve as a basis for harmonizing national and international regulations, while allowing flexibility to adapt to local needs. Governments and international organizations may adopt these regulations as mandatory or legally binding for the transport of dangerous goods. Compliance with these regulations is overseen by designated national authorities or independent bodies. The document also discusses international modal agreements, which adapt the UN Model Regulations for specific modes of transport, such as air, rail, road, sea, and postal services. For air transport, the ICAO Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air are legally binding and regularly updated. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) publishes Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR) that incorporate ICAO provisions and may include additional restrictions. For rail transport, the RID regulations apply in Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. Road transport is governed by the ADR agreement, applicable in 49 countries, with modified versions used in other regions. Sea transport follows the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code published by the International Maritime Organization (IMO). Postal services adhere to the UN Model Regulations, but high-risk infectious substances (Category A) are generally not accepted. National regulations often adopt the UN Model Regulations entirely or with variations to suit local conditions. Where national regulations do not exist, international modal agreements should be followed. In cases where multiple regulations apply to a single shipment, the most stringent ones should be applied. Operator or carrier variations may also exist, particularly in commercial transport industries. These variations, while not legally binding, may result in service refusal if not followed. Airlines and couriers may enforce additional safety requirements to maintain accountability and reputation. Failure to comply with these variations is a common reason for shipment delays or refusals. Supplementary regulations may apply to international transport, such as import/export licensing, storage permits, and agricultural or environmental safety regulations. It is the responsibility of the sender to ensure compliance with all applicable regulations. Special provisions address circumstances not covered by standard regulations, modifying or supplementing them to ensure the safe shipment of dangerous goods. Tables listing special provisions can be found in international regulation documents, including the UN Model Regulations. The document also outlines the responsibilities of various stakeholders in the transport process, including the sender, packaging supplier, and carrier. The sender is responsible for ensuring the package is prepared according to regulations, making arrangements with the carrier, and notifying the receiver of transportation details. The packaging supplier must manufacture and test materials according to regulations, provide test reports, and offer instructions for proper use. The carrier, which may include logistics companies, couriers, or airlines, must ensure compliance with applicable regulations and may impose additional safety requirements.
